title: [EN - LinkedIn] Read Karpathy nanochat before you rent a GPU
content:
A repo can say
the best chat model 100 dollars can buy.
That sentence is a title.
It is not a laptop demo.

The repo is github.com/karpathy/nanochat.
Andrej Karpathy's README.
The license on that README is MIT.
It is his training harness
for a small language model
on 1 GPU node.
It covers tokenization,
pretraining,
finetuning,
evaluation,
and a command-line chat.
It is not a wrapper
you paste into a coding agent
and call a product.

Read the dollar line
as his example, not as your invoice.
The README says a GPT-2 capability model,
which he says cost about 43,000 dollars
to train in 2019,
can be trained for 48 dollars.
He ties that 48 dollars
to about 2 hours
on an 8xH100 node.
He writes the rate he is using.
About 3 dollars per GPU per hour.
An 8xH100 node is then about 24 dollars an hour.
2 hours is about 48 dollars.
He also says a spot instance
can land closer to about 15 dollars.
Those are Karpathy's figures
on his README.
I am not repeating them
as a price I measured this week.
Rent the machine,
read the provider's price,
then do the multiplication yourself.

The leaderboard is the newer clock.
The README says the score to beat
is the original GPT-2 CORE score,
0.256525.
The table's row 6 is dated March 14, 2026.
It lists 1.65 hours,
a CORE score of 0.2626,
and the note autoresearch round 2.
The getting-started section says
runs/speedrun.sh takes about 1.5 hours.
The contributing section says
the same about 1.5 hours,
down from 3 hours.
The table and the prose
are not the same sentence.
If a clip says 48 dollars
and also says 1.65 hours,
those 2 lines describe
different durations.
Check the date on the row
before you repeat either number.

Here is the 1 dial he actually gives you.

The README says you set --depth,
the number of layers.
Other settings are computed from that.
The opening example says
GPT-2 capability is about depth 26.
Later he says the current code
sits around depth 24 to 26
for that grade.
Do not pick a depth off a thumbnail.
Open the README
on the day you run it.

The speedrun script
is written for an 8xH100 node.
He says the code also runs
on an 8xA100 node, slower.
On 1 GPU, he says you omit torchrun,
the results stay about the same,
and you wait about 8 times longer.
If the GPU has under 80 GB,
he says you will run out of memory
unless you lower --device-batch-size.
He lists the steps down.
32, then 16, 8, 4, 2, or 1.
Below that, he says
you need to know more
than the script is going to teach you.

There is a small-machine path,
and he warns you.
runs/runcpu.sh is the CPU
and Apple Silicon example.
He says it shrinks the model
so a run can finish
in a few 10 minutes.
He also says you will not get
strong results that way.
A Mac run is a smoke test
of the code, not the 48 dollar claim.

Say you do rent the 8xH100 box.
His setup uses uv.
For CUDA he writes
uv sync --extra gpu.
For CPU or MPS he writes
uv sync --extra cpu.
Then you activate the virtual environment.
Then bash runs/speedrun.sh.
He says to use a screen session
because the script takes
that hour-plus run.
After it finishes,
he says run
python -m scripts.chat_cli
with the environment still active.
He even tells you
to ask who you are,
because the small model will hallucinate.
Treat that chat
as a kindergarten-grade demo.
His word for the speedrun model
is a kindergartener.
It is not a stand-in
for a frontier model.

Here's my take.
Open the README before you rent.
Use his leaderboard date,
his stated hourly rate,
and the duration on the row you are copying.
The 48 dollar line is about 2 hours
at about 24 dollars an hour.
The March 14, 2026 row is 1.65 hours.
Those are NOT the same bill.
And a CPU script
is not the GPU result.

Follow for your daily AI update.
